title: Astika stops the fire
hookLine: a young sage, half from the snakes' own family, asks the king for one gift: stop the fire
carry: listening to the sacred story is itself devotion
tomorrow: what did a king in heaven do to get sent back down?
last: KARMA IS A CHAIN; KSHAMA CAN BREAK IT.

cards: The fire is lit. Janamejaya has heard how his father died, and his priests begin the snake sacrifice.
As they chant, snakes are drawn from everywhere into the flames, the text says, great and small, crying out as they fall. Takshaka, the one the king most wants, has fled to Indra for protection.
And a young man is walking toward the sacrifice, sent by his mother. His name is Astika. His father is a sage, his mother is the sister of a snake king, and he has come to stop the fire.

teach.h: A SAGE WHO WANTED NO WIFE.
teach.b: Astika's story starts with his father, a sage named Jaratkaru, who wanted no wife and no home. One day he found his ancestors hanging head down over a pit, holding a thin root that a rat was gnawing.
They were falling, they told him, because their line would end with him.

teach.h: A BRIDE WHO SHARED HIS NAME.
teach.b: So Jaratkaru agreed to marry, on strange terms: only a bride who shared his name. The snake king Vasuki had a sister named Jaratkaru, and he'd been told a child of this marriage would save the snakes.
That child is Astika. At the sacrifice, Astika doesn't argue or threaten. He praises the king, the priests and the fire, so well that Janamejaya wants to give him a gift.
Ask for anything, the king says. And Astika asks: stop the sacrifice. The king offers other gifts.
Astika holds to his one request. By now Takshaka is falling toward the flames, held in the air above them.
The assembly urges the king to keep his word, and Janamejaya does. The fire stops. Takshaka is spared.
And at this sacrifice, the text says, Vaishampayana tells the king his family's great story. So the frame closes on a king who came to burn and stayed to listen.
Hindus call that shravana, hearing, and the Bhagavata Purana names it first among the ways of devotion.

teach.h: LISTENING TO THE SACRED STORY IS ITSELF DEVOTION.
teach.b: That's why families still gather for katha, a sacred story told aloud over many evenings, and why the Mahabharata itself promises good to those who hear it. On the first day of this year we met him beside a fire.

how: Many Hindu families and temples hold katha: a sacred story, such as the Mahabharata, the Ramayana or the Bhagavata Purana, told or recited aloud, sometimes over many evenings, and hearing it is held to be devotion in itself. In some households Astika's name is remembered as a protection against snakes, in keeping with the promise the story records.

s: the Mahabharata begins as a story of revenge carried out
its frame ends with the revenge stopped: Janamejaya keeps his word and the fire goes out.
Janamejaya granted the request at once
he offered other gifts first; Astika held to his one request.
the fire stopped while he hung in the air above it.

games.q: your grandmother wants to tell the family a long scripture story after dinner, and your cousin wants to put on a show instead. by today's teaching, what fits?
o: listen; in Hindu practice, hearing the sacred story is itself devotion.
skip it; it only counts if you read it yourself, in Sanskrit.
listen for the plot, then look the rest up; the telling is just habit.
games.why: the frame ends with a king who stops his fire and sits down to hear his family's story. shravana, hearing, is named first among the ways of devotion; that's why families still gather for katha.

practice: For two minutes, just listen, without planning what you'll say back: to someone at home telling you about their day, to a recorded bhajan or chant, or to a few lines of a sacred text read aloud.
When your mind starts drafting a reply, set it down and go back to hearing. Janamejaya came to burn, and stayed to listen.
